blocks.text: Third, I do not understand why the Hebrews want זרזיר zarzir, that is, the sturnus [starling], to be a species of raven rather than the crow, the magpie, the jackdaw or the daw, which come closer to the nature of the raven. Yet Maimonides does not offer this on his own authority. For the Aruch cites it thus from the tractate Cholin, fol. 63: זה עורב למינה להביא את הזרזירין, this raven is said to be after its kind in order to designate the zarzirin (or starlings). There, however, I do not find the word הזרזירין, or of the starlings, today. But in Bava Kama, fol. 92 b, you may read a proverb that arose from it, which runs as follows: לא לחנם הלך זרזיר אצל עורב אלא מפני שהוא מינו, not for nothing does the starling go to the raven, since it is of the same species. And in Beresith Rabba, ch. 65, somewhat more briefly: לא הלך זרזיר אצל עורב אלא שהוא מינו, the starling would not go to the raven unless it were ὁμογενής [homogenēs]. And in Baal Hatturim the Cabbalists observe that the words עורב למינו, the raven after its kind, are by Gematria equal to זרזיר zarzir, for in Hebrew numerals each amounts to 414. And in Aquinas זרזיר zarzir is defined as עוף שהוא קרוב לצורת העורב, a bird which is similar in form to the raven. Nor is there any doubt that זרזיר zarzir is the starling. For in the Gloss on the Talmud it is explained as אשטו״רניל estournel; and in Pomarius, storno. And in Masal Kadmoni, Fable 51, the two speakers are called in Hebrew השפן והזרזיר, that is, the rabbit and the starling, as is clear from the picture. Finally, the Arabic زرزور [zarzūr] zarzour means the very same thing. Accordingly the words of Dioscorides in book 2, in the chapter On the dung of animals, ψαρὰς ὀρύζῃ τρέφοντες [psaras oryzē trephontes], feeding starlings on rice, were rendered by Avicenna in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter زبل [zibl], that is, On dung, as follows: الزرزور المتعلف للارز [al-zarzūr al-mutaʿallif li-l-aruzz] Zarzur fed on rice: that is, the starling, not the thrush, as the Latin translators rendered it, by an error that arose in Spain, where zorzal is the thrush.

Less familiar is the word שרנקא sarneka, which Maimonides uses for a species of נץ nets, or hawk, as the Talmudists use שורינקא sorinka, and, what is the same, בר־חיריא bar-chirja. The words run thus in the tractate Cholin, in the place cited above: ת״ר הנץ [III, 121] זה הנץ למינהו להביא את בר־חיריא מאי בר־חיריא אמר אביי שורינקא Our masters have taught that the hawk is said to be after its kind so as to signify bar-chirja. What is bar-chirja? Abji said: It is forinka. The Aruch reads [col. 354] בר־חוריא bar-churja, and שורניקא sornika. And in Arabic, in Giggeius, سرنوق [surnūq] surnouk is a bird of the hawk kind, living by prey. I am mistaken if this is not the same bird that Damir calls in one copy شروق [shrwq] saruk, in the other زرق [zurraq] zurrak, of which Ibno-Saida says thus: طاير يصاد به بين البازي والباشق [ṭāyir yuṣād bihi bayna al-bāzī wa-l-bāshiq] It is a bird used in fowling, intermediate (that is, of intermediate size) between Albazi and Albasak, species of hawk very well known among the Arabs. And Alphera: هو البازي الابيض والجمع الزرارق وهو صنف من البازي لطيف الا ان مزجه احر وايبس ولذلك هو اشد جناحا واسرع طيرانا واقوي اقداما وفيه ختل وخبث وخير الوانه الاسود الظهر الابيض الصدر الاحمر العين [huwa al-bāzī al-abyaḍ wa-l-jamʿ al-zarāriq wa-huwa ṣinf min al-bāzī laṭīf illā anna mizājahu aḥarr wa-aybas wa-li-dhālika huwa ashadd janāḥan wa-asraʿ ṭayarānan wa-aqwā aqdāman wa-fīhi khatl wa-khubth wa-khayr alwānihi al-aswad al-ẓahr al-abyaḍ al-ṣadr al-aḥmar al-ʿayn] It is Albazi (or the white hawk). The plural is zerariko. It is an elegant species of hawk, but of a very hot and very dry temperament. And therefore it is stronger in its wings, swifter in flight, and stronger in its feet. And in it there is cunning and malice, and excellence of colour. For it is black on the back, white on the breast, red in the eye. From the whiteness of its breast it is called by the Talmudists בר־חוריא, son of whiteness. It should be examined whether it is the white falcon of more recent writers.
